phonemes.desc: Single syllable with voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l], final [ʊŋ] (close-mid back rounded vowel + velar nasal), and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'o' before 'ng' corresponds to IPA [ʊ].

pronunciation.approximation: LUHNG — the 'o' is like the 'oo' in 'book', and the tone rises from mid to high, as in a questioning intonation.

kin.label: Related terms
kin.form: 龍王 Lóngwáng (Dragon King); 龍門 Lóngmén (Dragon Gate)

pronunciation.note: 龍 denotes the Chinese dragon, an emblem of imperial authority, fertility, and cosmic yang force. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is lóng (Tone 2), as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard Mandarin dictionaries. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese form as *[m]-roŋ (GSR 1193a). The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Lóng preserves the citation rising tone of the second tone; in connected speech the contour may be compressed, but the lexical tone remains Tone 2.

domains.title: Sovereign of Rivers and Rain
domains.subtitle: Imperial Power, Fertility, Cosmic Yang
domains.lead:
Lóng is not the fire-breathing tyrant of Western fairy tales. The Chinese dragon is a composite being — antlers of a stag, head of a camel, eyes of a demon, neck of a snake, belly of a clam, scales of a carp, claws of an eagle, pads of a tiger — and yet it moves as a single fluid force. It is the spirit of water in all its forms: the river, the rain, the mist, and the storm. It is also the imperial emblem of absolute legitimacy, the yang counterweight to the phoenix's yin, and the power that makes the fields fertile.

Wherever Chinese civilization spread, the dragon went with it: carved on jade, coiled around columns, embroidered on silk, and raised above temples as a promise that heaven still listened.

cards.name: Water and Weather
cards.desc: Dragons command rivers, lakes, clouds, and rain; drought is read as the dragon's withdrawal, flood as its untimely arrival.

cards.name: Imperial Authority
cards.desc: The five-clawed dragon was reserved for the Son of Heaven; to usurp it was treason, to bear it legitimately was the mandate of heaven.

cards.name: The Pearl of Wisdom
cards.desc: The dragon chasing a flaming pearl symbolizes the pursuit of enlightenment, potency, and the luminous source of all things.

cards.name: Cosmic Yang
cards.desc: As the active, ascending, bright principle, the dragon pairs with the phoenix to model the complementary dynamism of the cosmos.

symbols.name: Dragon pearl
symbols.meaning: Wisdom, spiritual energy, and the moon or sun the dragon protects

symbols.name: Antlers and horns
symbols.meaning: Vitality, longevity, and the stag-like generative power of nature

symbols.name: Carp scales
symbols.meaning: Transformation — the carp that leaps the Dragon Gate becomes a dragon

symbols.name: Clouds and waves
symbols.meaning: The dragon's medium; it does not fly through air but swims through mist and rain

symbols.name: Five claws
symbols.meaning: Imperial supremacy; fewer claws marked nobility or vassal states

mythology.lead: Chinese dragon lore is less a single narrative than a vast ecology of stories — about weather, examinations, bureaucracy, and the sky itself. The lóng is not born but achieved: a fish that leaps, a rain that answers petition, a constellation that keeps the seasons. These four episodes map its four habitats: myth, folklore, religion, and the stars.

myths.title: Yinglong, the Winged Dragon
myths.text: The oldest dragon of record is a war-machine of rain. When the Yellow Emperor faced the rebel Chiyou at Zhuolu — the battle that made Chinese kingship — Chiyou raised a fog so thick that day became night and the imperial armies lost their way. The compass-chariot answered the fog, and Yinglong, the winged dragon, answered Chiyou: 'Yinglong slew Chiyou, and afterwards slew Kuafu' (Shanhaijing, 'Great Wilderness: North'). The later poem asks the pointed question: 'How did Yinglong mark out the land? By what did the rivers come to run?' (Chuci, 'Heavenly Questions') — the dragon's body becoming geography, rivers traced by the coils of its tail. Yinglong's biography is the biography of Chinese statecraft in miniature: heaven sends rain, rain serves the throne, and the dragon is the treaty between them, sealed at the founding battle.

myths.title: The Carp at Dragon Gate
myths.text: Every spring the carp of the Yellow River run upstream past the rapids called Longmen, 'Dragon Gate', the cleft the Great Yu was said to have cut through the mountain. Few survive the leap; those that do are transformed into dragons. The story is first recorded in the lost geography Sanqin ji (三秦記, 'Account of the Three Qin'), known through quotations in later encyclopedias such as the Taiping Yulan — and it gave Chinese its standard metaphor for examination success: lǐyú tiào lóngmén, 'the carp leaps the Dragon Gate'. For two thousand years the phrase carried the hopes of farming families: a boy who passed the jinshi examinations transformed his lineage as completely as a fish changes its element. The myth quietly defines the dragon itself — not a breed but a rank, an estate reached through effort, upstream, against the current, at the one gate in the world where water and heaven touch.

myths.title: The Dragon Kings of the Four Seas
myths.text: With Buddhism came the nāgas — serpent-kings of waters and treasure — and China answered with its own bureaucracy of the deep: the Four Dragon Kings who rule the seas at the four quarters and answer for rain. Their temples line the coasts and riverbanks; in drought, officials led processions to the Dragon King shrine to petition for clouds, and a temple that failed to deliver rain could be, in legend and occasionally in fact, punished. The best known of them, Ao Guang of the Eastern Sea, meets the reader twice in the Ming novels: in Investiture of the Gods the boy Nezha beats his third son and humiliates the king himself, forcing him to petition Heaven; in Journey to the West (ch. 3) the monkey Sun Wukong invades his palace and arms himself from the deep treasury. The Dragon Kings are the comic register of an ancient awe: the ocean as a court, complete with armies, ledgers, treasures — and a grievance procedure even the gods must answer.

myths.title: The Azure Dragon of the East
myths.text: Qīnglóng, the Azure Dragon, guards the eastern quarter of the sky — one of the Four Symbols that anchor Chinese cosmology, alongside the White Tiger of the West, the Vermilion Bird of the South, and the Dark Tortoise of the North. The Huainanzi, in its 'Treatise on Celestial Patterns', maps the correspondence system: east is wood, wood is spring, spring is the azure dragon, and the dragon's voice is the year's first thunder. Star atlases draw the beast across seven lunar mansions of the eastern horizon — from Horn to Tail — its sinuous body built from stars that Greek astronomy filed under Scorpius and Libra. Under this sign the Han emperors aligned gates and founded observatories; the Azure Dragon is where astronomy stops being foreign and becomes the calendar of sowing. When the first spring thunder sounds over the fields, the old texts say, the dragon has turned in its sleep — and the year has begun.

lore.syncretism: The Chinese dragon absorbed and influenced dragon imagery across East Asia. The Japanese ryū and tatsu, the Korean yong, and the Vietnamese rồng all descend from the same visual and cosmological root, though each culture adjusted claw count, temperament, and color symbolism. Indian nāgas — serpent deities of water and the underworld — entered China with Buddhism and were often depicted as dragon-like guardians, especially in rain-making ritual and at temple gates. The Western dragon is a distinct tradition: a hoarding, fire-breathing antagonist shaped by Near Eastern and medieval European warfare, only superficially related to the Chinese rain-bringing sovereign. Modern global culture often conflates the two, but they answer to different cosmologies — one guards gold in a cave, the other brings the rain that fills the rice bowl.
lore.culturalLegacy: The dragon never left Chinese public life. The Qing imperial flag was a five-clawed dragon on a yellow field; the Republic and early People's Republic used dragon motifs on currency, stamps, and regalia. Today the dragon dance winds through Lunar New Year streets worldwide, and the Year of the Dragon is the most auspicious sign in the zodiac. In feng shui, dragon imagery channels qi; in martial arts, styles such as Dragon Shape imitate its coiling power; in language, lóng compounds mark excellence — lóngfèng (dragon and phoenix) for harmonious marriage, wàngzǐlóng for the hope of sons. The dragon has also become a contested nationalist symbol — claimed by state propaganda, diaspora communities, and pop culture alike as the badge of Chinese identity and ancestral continuity. Restoring Lóng with its tone mark returns the rise in pitch that the character 龍 has carried for three thousand years.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The Chinese dragon teaches that power need not be hard. It is water made conscious: yielding enough to flow around any obstacle, forceful enough to wear down mountains. Unlike the Western dragon guarding a static hoard, the Chinese dragon is process — rain becoming river, river becoming mist, mist returning to cloud. It is a reminder that sovereignty in the Chinese imagination is less about domination than about maintaining the dynamic balance that lets life flourish.

To name a domain Lóng is therefore to claim something older than empire: the claim that the cosmos itself pulses with living, transformative energy. The dragon does not ask to be worshipped from a distance; it asks to be recognized in the rain on the field, the mist on the mountain, and the long coiling body of a river moving toward the sea — power that arrives, feeds everything it touches, and leaves.

lore.archaeology: The earliest dragon image in China may be the C-shaped jade 'pig-dragon' of the Hongshan culture (c. 4700–2900 BCE) from Inner Mongolia and Liaoning; the Erlitou culture (c. 1900–1500 BCE) produced a turquoise-inlaid dragon plaque; Shang and Zhou bronzes coil dragon-derived taotie masks across their surfaces. Han dynasty tomb murals and stone reliefs show dragons pulling chariots, guarding ascents to immortality, and arching between earth and heaven. Textually the dragon is present from the oracle-bone inscriptions onward, already a royal and meteorological sign by the Western Zhou — three thousand years of continuous iconography for a creature that was never alive and never stopped acting.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 龍 in traditional Chinese and 龙 in simplified. Pinyin Lóng (Tone 2) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries. The registrable Unicode restoration uses tone-marked Pinyin rather than the hanzi because PUNICODEX renders the original character in the temple's 'Original Script' card while keeping the domain label pronounceable and internationally registrable. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese form as *[m]-roŋ.
